reports.title: Pueblo’s 2026 adopted budget: what the ordinance actually authorizes
reports.stage: SOURCE-BACKED EXPLANATORY BRIEF · NOT AN EXPENDITURE AUDIT
reports.review: Source-backed figures; independently reproduced accounting audit pending
reports.summary: The City adopted a $128,202,143 General Fund appropriation for fiscal 2026 under Ordinance 11075. This is an adopted spending authorization, not evidence that every appropriated dollar has been paid.
whatKnown: Ordinance 11075 adopts the FY2026 city budget and states the General Fund revenue and department appropriation schedule.
The Finance Department separately lists a 2027 proposed budget. A proposal is not an enacted appropriation or a verified payment.
The 2026 State of the City describes a revenue outlook and service pressures; that narrative must be read as an administration statement and reconciled against financial statements.
unknowns: FY2026 actual disbursements and audited year-end results were not reconciled for this brief.
The 2027 proposal may change through Council action; do not label its amounts as adopted before reviewing final ordinances.
Different budget documents may group funds differently; avoid comparing citywide and General Fund numbers as though they share a denominator.
reports.who: City Council adopts budget ordinances; the Mayor submits an executive proposal; the Finance Department keeps official financial records. Specific charter authority and any amendments must be checked against source instruments.
reports.what: General Fund FY2026 adopted budget and associated revenue estimates.
reports.when: FY2026 appropriation, adopted under Ordinance 11075; this explanatory brief prepared November 9, 2026.
reports.where: City of Pueblo, Colorado; General Fund scope, not all entities in Pueblo County.
reports.why: Budget authorizations determine available public spending and services; households need to distinguish proposed, authorized and actually spent amounts.
reports.how: Compare the adopted ordinance with later monthly financial statements, treasury outflows, amendments, staffing changes and audited ACFR.

money.detail: Mayor’s proposal; can be amended before adoption.
FY2026 General Fund appropriation: $128,202,143.
Contracts and purchase orders create separate commitments.
Payments require actual transaction or audited expenditure evidence.
Services, employment and community results require independent measures.

relations: Direct: City Council approval, Finance Department budget implementation, departments receiving appropriations.
Second order: contractors, service providers, unions, nonprofits and capital projects affected by allocations.
Third order: residents’ services, long-term operating commitments, household and child impacts; impacts are hypotheses until measured.
reports.counter: Adoption of a budget is not itself evidence of money being misspent. An apparent difference between proposals and final appropriations may reflect amendments or accounting classifications.
options: Publish adopted versus amended versus actual FY2026 tables, with clear fund scope.
Create a 2027 proposal-to-adoption change log by meeting, ordinance and vote.
Track cost reductions alongside observed service levels and resident impacts rather than assuming either success or failure.
reports.child: Potential service effects for children and families should be traced to program budgets and measured delivery, without profiling minors.
reports.ee: Compare review time, source availability and accounting effort before deeper forensic work; do not claim an EE score without measured inputs.
reports.t2y: Truth stage: adopted ordinance supports the appropriation figure. Useful-yield stage: residents can compare authority and actuals once spending records are reconciled. Publication remains human-reviewed.
reports.rx: Preserve original and amended budgets, archived ordinances and dated reconciliations; flag contradictory totals for review.
actions: Use the City’s annual budget and financial transparency portal to inspect expenditure records.
For any disputed line, record department, fund, budget year, accounting stage, document URL and last verification date.
Request a public-record crosswalk before alleging misuse or predicting program effects.

The underlying expenditures, delivery milestones and achieved employment outcomes need separate records.

reports.what: Economic Development Half-Cent Tax Fund, future commitments in April 2026 report.
reports.when: April reporting period; reported data as of May 13, 2026; Qified brief November 9, 2026.

relations: Direct: Council approval, Finance Fund accounting and named project code.
Second order: eligible projects, infrastructure contractors, industrial site users and operating agencies.
Third order: public services, opportunities for workers and household effects; all require case-specific evidence.
reports.counter: A commitment is not automatically an improper expense or an actual cash payment. Infrastructure spending can serve multiple projects, so allocations require a defensible methodology and no double counting.

Show changes between April 2026 and the latest available economic-development report.
For debated projects, assign infrastructure costs on transparent criteria and disclose alternate allocations.

reports.title: 2027 nonprofit funding: requests versus proposed City support
reports.stage: SOURCE-ATTRIBUTED DEVELOPING ISSUE · MULTI-PARTY REVIEW OPEN
reports.review: City statement is source-attributed; independent county counterstatement and final awards not reconciled
reports.summary: The City of Pueblo reports approximately $2.2 million in 2027 nonprofit funding requests from 46 organizations, while its 2027 proposed budget includes $490,000 for CSAC. That proposed allocation remains subject to Council approval. A request, proposed allocation, recommendation and award are different stages.
whatKnown: The City’s September 2026 release states that 46 applications were received and cautions that applications are not awards.
A later City release states its 2027 proposed budget includes $490,000 for CSAC; the City describes a dispute over County participation and reimbursement.
The source release describes CSAC as an established City–County recommendation process.
unknowns: Actual approved 2027 City and County awards, if any, and the results of later deliberations.
Independent reconciliation of the County’s position on funding and any reimbursements.
Which applicants meet eligibility standards and what service levels a given grant would purchase.
reports.who: Community Services Advisory Commission evaluates nonprofit applications; City and County decision-making bodies have their own funding authority.
reports.what: 2027 nonprofit application pipeline, proposed City funding and disputed intergovernmental arrangements.
reports.when: Applications announced September 2026; City funding statement published in early November 2026.
reports.where: Pueblo regional nonprofit service organizations; allocations and jurisdiction should be recorded separately.
reports.why: Funding decisions may affect social services; stakeholders need clear amounts, conditions, timing and official decisions.
reports.how: Compare the published application ledger to CSAC scores/recommendations, both governments’ votes and final grant agreements.

money.detail: Approximately $2.2 million submitted by 46 organizations.
City says $490,000 in proposed 2027 CSAC budget.
CSAC recommendations require deliberation.
City/County approvals and award letters needed.
Actual grant disbursements require transaction records.

relations: Direct: applicant nonprofits, CSAC and appropriating governments.
Second order: staff, subcontractors and providers that deliver funded services.
Third order: vulnerable residents and long-term service impacts; protect individual identities.
reports.counter: The City’s description of County withdrawal and the reimbursement disagreement is the City’s position in a public statement, not a neutral finding of responsibility. A request-to-proposal funding gap alone does not identify which programs qualify.
options: Publish a program-by-program application, recommendation, award and payment ledger, with appeal/correction routes.
Compare service-continuity scenarios for reduced, delayed and full funding while protecting confidential client data.
Document both City and County responses and the executed funding arrangements before assigning fault.
reports.child: Childcare, nutrition, elder support and housing-service impacts should be analyzed at program level with privacy protections; no child is profiled.
reports.ee: Use one cross-government reconciliation and reusable program-level data model rather than repeated manual comparisons.
reports.t2y: Source-backed request and proposal amounts are useful, but the actual award and service outcomes remain undetermined and must not be predicted as facts.
reports.rx: Maintain dated releases and recommendations, publish revised grant decisions and keep a clear correction history.
actions: Review the published application list and official funding statement.
Check subsequent CSAC recommendations and each governing body’s appropriation votes.
Ask how service continuity and independent oversight are protected if funding is reduced.

whatKnown: The dashboard divides 26 priorities into eight portfolios: Financial Strategy (4), Correctional Services & Safety Support (4), Workforce & Organization (4), Growth & Development (6), Economic Development (1), Infrastructure (4), Housing (2), Human Services (1).

The three items marked waiting are debris removal program, public roads and bridges dashboard, and detention center solar PPA.
The August financial priorities—2025 audit close, 2026 budget amendment, standing financial reporting, and grant management system—are each marked underway.
unknowns: Whether a later Board action or operational change altered any August status.
Contracts, exact funding, cash payments, performance outcomes and individual legal owners for each program.
Whether any County-listed relationship has enforceable terms; the dashboard alone cannot establish that.
reports.who: The Pueblo County Board of County Commissioners sets the published priorities and reviews them with its Chief Administrative Officer, according to the County dashboard. Individual contractors and grant custodians require separate records.
reports.what: 26 County initiatives across eight portfolios; not City Council projects.
reports.when: Dashboard displays August 8, 2026 as its update; checked November 9, 2026.
reports.where: Pueblo County, Colorado; County government and partner agencies, not City of Pueblo.
reports.why: The County says the dashboard provides residents a public view of Board priorities and their progress.
reports.how: Read the portfolio and status for each initiative. Corroborate material funding, contracts and achieved outcomes in Board agendas, executed agreements, financial reports and delivery evidence.

money.detail: 26 published initiatives (1 Complete, 22 Underway, 3 Waiting).
No comprehensive initiative-by-initiative appropriations in dashboard summary.
Debris removal procurement marked waiting; no award established in snapshot.
money.status: Check Board resolutions and purchasing records.

Distinguish County, City and special-district responsibilities.

whatKnown: The City adopted Ordinance 11074 on November 24, 2025, with mayoral approval dated November 26, 2025.
The ordinance certifies 15.633 gross City mills for the 2026 budget year.
The accompanying background estimates property-tax revenue of $21,280,697, net of estimated uncollectible taxes. The adopted levy rate is reported as the same as in 2025.

reports.where: Taxable property within City of Pueblo, Colorado.
reports.why: To support the City's general operating expenditures.
reports.how: Municipal component is assessed taxable value multiplied by 15.633 / 1000, subject to actual parcel assessment, exemptions and applicable rules.
